passage: Theories of punishment have long been divided between those that look forward and those that look back. Forward-looking theories justify punishment by its effects: it deters, it incapacitates, perhaps it reforms. Their persistent embarrassment is that they seem to license too much. If the point of punishment were simply to discourage crime, then punishing an innocent person whom the public believed guilty might serve that point as well as punishing the guilty one, and sometimes better, since it would be quicker. Most people regard this conclusion as monstrous, which suggests that the effects of punishment, however important, cannot be the whole of its justification.

An expressive theory offers to supply what is missing. On this view punishment is, before anything else, a form of communication: the community's way of declaring that an act was wrong and that the person who did it is answerable for it. This explains at once why the innocent may not be punished. To condemn someone who did nothing is not an inefficient use of punishment but a lie told in its language. It also explains why we distinguish a fine from a tax, though both take money: the tax carries no message of blame, while the fine carries little else.

The obvious objection is that condemnation can be expressed in words. If the point of a prison sentence is to say that an act was wrong, why not simply say so, in a formal judgement solemnly delivered? The expressive theorist's reply is that words alone are too cheap to carry the message. A declaration that costs the offender nothing would be heard as a declaration that the wrong did not matter much; only something that is felt as a burden registers the seriousness of what was done.

This reply is ingenious, but it has an uncomfortable implication. If hard treatment communicates because of the meanings a society attaches to it, then how much hard treatment is needed depends on those meanings, and meanings can drift. A society accustomed to long sentences will hear a short one as a shrug; the same sentence elsewhere might sound like thunder. The expressive theory, in other words, cannot by itself tell us how severe punishment should be, because severity is fixed by convention, and conventions can escalate without limit. That is not a reason to abandon the theory, which captures something the forward-looking view plainly misses. It is a reason to think that the theory needs a partner: some independent principle, perhaps of proportion or of humanity, that sets limits the language of condemnation cannot set for itself.

options.A: Where courts declare offenders guilty but impose no penalty, the public judges those offences as serious as ones punished by imprisonment.
options.B: Fines that are very small relative to an offender's wealth tend to be treated by offenders as a routine cost of doing business.
options.C: Long prison sentences do less to reduce reoffending than shorter sentences combined with close supervision after release.
options.D: Judges in different countries tend to deliver their verdicts in quite different styles and in very different forms of language.

passage: Why does a string quartet cost so much more to hear today, relative to a shirt or a radio, than it did a century ago? Not because the musicians have become greedy or the concert halls inefficient. Performing a quartet required four players and roughly forty minutes then, and it requires the same now; no innovation has allowed three musicians to play it in half the time without destroying the thing being bought. Meanwhile workers in manufacturing have become many times more productive, and their wages have risen accordingly. The musicians' pay must rise too, or they would drift into other work. So the price of the quartet climbs relative to goods whose production has been transformed, even though nothing about the quartet has changed.

Economists sometimes call this the cost disease, and its reach goes far beyond concert halls. Teaching, nursing, care of the elderly and much legal and administrative work share the quartet's structure: the service largely consists of a person's time and attention, and attempts to compress that time often degrade what is delivered. A class of sixty is cheaper per pupil than a class of thirty, but it is not the same product at a lower price. Where productivity in such sectors lags, their share of national spending rises, and with it a persistent suspicion that schools and hospitals are squandering money, since nearly everything else seems to be getting cheaper.

The diagnosis contains a consolation that is often missed. If the relative cost of services rises because the rest of the economy has become more productive, then society as a whole is richer, and can afford those services even at their higher relative price. A family that spends a larger share of its income on its children's schooling than its grandparents did may also own far more and work fewer hours. What feels like a crisis of affordability is, on this view, partly a change in the composition of a growing budget.

The argument should not be stretched into a blanket excuse. That some cost growth in services is unavoidable does not mean that all of it is; administrative layers can multiply in a hospital as easily as in any other organisation, and the cost disease offers them no defence. Nor is the consolation automatic. The higher relative price of care falls hardest on those whose incomes have not shared in the general gain, and public budgets that depend on taxes voters resist may cut services long before the arithmetic says they must. The cost disease explains a pattern; it does not settle who should pay for it.

options.A: manufacturing productivity may one day stop growing, which would remove the cause of the cost disease.
options.B: the higher relative price of care weighs most on people whose incomes have not shared in the general gain.
options.C: public budgets that depend on unpopular taxes may cut services well before the arithmetic of affordability requires it.
options.D: rising relative costs in a service may partly reflect administrative growth that the cost disease does not excuse.

passage: For much of the twentieth century, anthropologists sorted the ties they recorded into two kinds. Some were 'real', resting on birth and descent; others were 'fictive', a convenient label for godparents, sworn brothers, adopted children and the many other relations that people treated as kinship but that did not, so the observer thought, rest on blood. The distinction seemed merely descriptive, and it took some time to see that it carried a theory with it: that the true foundation of kinship is biological, and that everything else is imitation.

The difficulty is that many of the people being described did not share the theory. In a number of societies, people become kin by eating food grown on the same land, by living in the same house, or by being nursed at the same breast. Under Islamic law, for instance, children nursed by the same woman are barred from marrying one another, much as siblings by birth would be; the tie created by milk is not a metaphor for kinship but a form of it. In such places, ties made in these ways may carry the same obligations of help, hospitality and mourning as ties of birth. Where relatedness is understood to accumulate through feeding and sharing over years, to call such ties fictive is not to describe them but to overrule the people who live them.

This is not an argument that biology is irrelevant. Birth is, almost everywhere, one of the most powerful ways of reckoning who belongs to whom, and an attempt to dissolve it entirely into choice would be its own kind of distortion. The point is narrower: biology is one idiom of relatedness among several, and which idioms count, and how much, varies from place to place. Nor is the West an exception that proves the biological rule. Adoption, the blended families formed by remarriage, and the arrangements made possible by donated eggs and sperm all require people to decide, often painfully, whether a tie of birth or a tie of care should prevail when the two come apart.

Seen this way, kinship is something people do as well as something they are born into. The older vocabulary was not useless, since it pointed to real differences in the ways ties are formed and maintained. Its error lay in treating one culture's answer to the question of what makes people kin as the standard against which every other answer was to be measured, and in mistaking that answer for a fact of nature rather than a choice that other peoples had made differently.

options.A: making their home together in the same house.
options.B: inheriting a share of the same land from a common ancestor.
options.C: being nursed as infants by the same woman.
options.D: eating food that has been grown on the same land.

passage: It has become a commonplace, in philosophy as much as in popular psychology, that a self is a kind of story. On this view a person is not a thing that persists beneath her experiences but the narrative she composes from them: the account of where she came from, what she has struggled against and where she is heading. The claim is usually advanced in two forms at once. The descriptive form says that human beings do in fact understand themselves through stories. The normative form adds that they ought to, and that a life which cannot be gathered into a coherent narrative is in some way impoverished or broken.

The descriptive claim is plausible for many people, but its generality is doubtful. Some people report that they do not experience their lives as a plot at all. They feel little connection with the person they were a decade ago, find the invitation to tell their life story faintly baffling, and live with their attention fixed on present tasks and relationships. Nor is there any obvious sense in which their lives go worse: they form attachments, deliberate carefully and take responsibility for their conduct, only without experiencing their existence as an unfolding plot. It would be rash to assume that such people are simply unreflective, or that they are concealing a narrative they would rather not acknowledge. Their testimony is at least as credible as that of people who say the opposite, and it suggests that narrative self-understanding is one way of being a self rather than the condition of being one.

The normative claim is more troubling. Stories have shapes, and the pressure to give one's life a shape is a pressure to select. Episodes that fit the arc are remembered and retold; those that do not are discarded or reinterpreted. Autobiographical memory is already reconstructive, and a governing narrative supplies it with a principle of selection that is rarely examined. A person who has told herself for years that she is someone who overcomes adversity will find it difficult to see the occasions on which she gave up, and harder still to learn from them. The demand for coherence can thus become a demand for a flattering kind of forgetting. A novelist may legitimately omit whatever does not serve the plot; a life conducted on the same principle may lose precisely the evidence it most needs.

None of this means that narrative has no place. Making a promise requires regarding one's future self as continuous with one's present intention, and recovering from bereavement or injury often involves finding a way to tell what happened so that it can be lived with. Understanding other people, too, frequently depends on grasping the story they take themselves to be in. These are genuine goods, and a person who could never assemble any part of her past into an account would be at a real disadvantage.

But the goods enumerated here are those of an instrument, not of an essence. We use stories to bind ourselves, to heal and to understand, and we can use them well or badly, often or seldom. To say that the self simply is its story makes the instrument indispensable, and it turns a difference in temperament into a deficiency. The more modest view leaves room both for lives that are lived largely in the present and for the episodes that refuse to fit, and it may well be the more truthful of the two.

options.A: regards living by stories and living in the present as mere differences of temperament, neither better than the other.
options.B: shows that temperament rather than narrative is what a person's self really consists in.
options.C: explains differences of temperament between people as the outcome of the better or worse life stories they have told.
options.D: treats people who do not live by stories as lacking something when they merely differ in disposition.

passage: Quantum theory is among the most precisely confirmed bodies of physics ever constructed, and it is also, by the admission of many who use it, a theory that does not quite say what it is about. The difficulty is usually called the measurement problem. The theory's central equation describes a system by a mathematical object, the wave function, which evolves smoothly and predictably for as long as nobody looks. Under that evolution a particle can come to be in a combination, or superposition, of possibilities: here and there, spinning one way and the other. Yet whenever an experimenter checks, the apparatus records exactly one result. The textbook rule bridges the gap by decree: at the moment of measurement the wave function 'collapses' to one of the possibilities, with probabilities that the theory supplies.

The trouble is that the rule invokes a notion the theory never defines. A measuring device is made of atoms, and atoms obey the smooth equation; treated as part of the physical system, the device should itself enter a superposition of having recorded each result, rather than recording one. Somewhere between the particle and the experimenter's notebook the smooth evolution is supposed to give way to the abrupt one, but the theory does not say where, or why, or what counts as a measurement in the first place. In practice nothing hangs on the answer, because the boundary can be drawn anywhere convenient without altering the predicted statistics. That is precisely what makes the problem so easy to ignore.

The proposed solutions divide, roughly, by what they are prepared to give up. Some modify the smooth equation, adding a tiny spontaneous tendency to collapse that is negligible for single particles but overwhelming for anything as large as a pointer. Others leave the equation untouched and deny that collapse ever happens: every possible outcome is realised, each in a branch of reality that cannot interact with the others, and the appearance of a single result is simply what being in one branch is like. Still others add a further ingredient to the wave function, definite positions for particles at all times, guided by the wave, so that the outcome was settled all along. A widely discussed physical process, in which a system's entanglement with its surroundings rapidly suppresses the signs of superposition, is often offered as a solution in its own right; it explains why superpositions of large objects are never seen, but on most accounts it does not explain why one outcome occurs rather than another.

Because these rival pictures agree, in nearly every experiment so far performed, with each other and with the textbook rule, a common response is to call the dispute metaphysics, a matter of taste for people who have finished their calculations. The response is understandable but confused. It treats the textbook rule as a neutral baseline from which the interpretations depart, when the rule is itself an interpretation, and an incomplete one, since it relies on a word it cannot define. Nor are the rivals strictly equivalent: the theories that modify the equation predict small departures from standard behaviour in sufficiently large systems, and experiments of increasing delicacy are now searching for them.

None of this obliges the working physicist to choose a side before computing a reaction rate; the theory's practical success is real, and it does not wait on the outcome of the debate. But a theory that works without our knowing what it describes has not thereby been shown to need no description. The measurement problem is not a puzzle from philosophy grafted onto physics. It is a gap in the statement of the physics itself, one that the theory's very success has made easy to step around.

options.A: The measurement problem would vanish if experiments confirmed that all the rival pictures make identical predictions.
options.B: The chief defect the author finds in the textbook rule would be removed if the theory stated precisely what counts as a measurement.
options.C: Physicists ought to settle which interpretation is correct before they rely on the predictions that the theory makes.
options.D: The interpretations that leave the equation untouched are to be preferred, because they alone avoid an undefined notion of measurement.

passage: When a dominant company is overtaken by a newcomer, the explanation usually offered is some version of complacency: its managers, the story goes, grew comfortable, stopped listening to the market and failed to perceive what was approaching. The story has the appeal of a fable, and it permits the rest of us to believe that an identical fate could be avoided simply by remaining vigilant. Its difficulty is that, in many of the best known cases, the incumbent's managers were neither lazy nor blind. They were doing, carefully and well, exactly what they had been trained to do.

The pattern runs roughly as follows. A new technology appears that is, at first, worse than the existing one by the measures that the incumbent's best customers care about. It is slower, or less precise, or less durable, but it is cheaper and simpler, and it finds a small market among buyers who were never well served by the established product. The incumbent asks its customers whether they want the new thing, and they say no. It examines the margins, and they are thin. It looks at the size of the market, and it is too small to move a company of its scale. Every one of these judgements is correct, and together they lead the firm to put its money where its profits are. Meanwhile the new technology improves, year by year, until it is good enough for the mainstream, and the incumbent discovers that its careful attention to its best customers has left it with nothing to offer the rest.

It may be objected that this account is written with the convenient clarity of hindsight, since for every cheap technology that grew up to displace its betters, many others remained toys and disappeared, and an incumbent that chased all of them would have squandered its resources. The objection is fair, but it strengthens rather than weakens the point. If good managers cannot tell in advance which small markets will matter, then vigilance alone cannot be the remedy, because the problem is not a failure to look but a set of rules for deciding what is worth looking at.

What seems to help is therefore structural rather than psychological: firms that have survived such transitions have often placed the new venture in a separate unit, with its own costs and its own measures of success, small enough that a small market can still excite it. This is no guarantee, since separate units can be starved or smothered by the parent organisation, but the arrangement at least removes the new business from the scrutiny of the rules that would have judged it, correctly by their own lights, not worth the trouble.

options.A: its engineers lack the technical skills needed to work with the newer and simpler design.
options.B: the market for the new technology is too small to matter to a company of its scale.
options.C: its existing customers, when asked about the new technology, say that they do not want it.
options.D: the profit margins it could earn from selling the new technology look thin when examined.

passage: In most schools a test is understood as a thermometer. It is applied at the end of a period of learning to find out how much has been learned, and like a thermometer it is supposed to leave the thing it measures unchanged. The understanding is so familiar that it seldom occurs to anyone that it might be false. Yet one of the more robust findings in the psychology of memory is that the act of retrieving something from memory is not a neutral reading: it changes the memory, and generally strengthens it, so that material which has been recalled once is more likely to be recalled again than material which has merely been seen again.

The contrast is clearest when the two activities are set against each other. Suppose two groups of students study the same passage, after which one group rereads it while the other closes the book and writes down whatever it can remember. The design holds constant both the material and the time spent on it, so that the only difference between the groups is whether they looked at the passage again or tried to bring it back unaided. Tested a few minutes later, the rereaders often do as well or better; tested a week later, the group that practised recall tends to remember considerably more. The advantage of retrieval, in other words, is easily hidden by the timing of the measurement, which may be one reason why it was overlooked for so long by teachers and students alike.

What is more striking is how little the students themselves sense any of this. Asked to predict their own performance, rereaders tend to be the more confident group. Rereading produces a feeling of fluency, in which the sentences are familiar and slide past easily, and ease of processing is readily mistaken for mastery. Attempting recall produces the opposite feeling, since it is effortful, it exposes gaps and it is often unpleasant, which is presumably why students left to themselves so rarely choose it. Teachers are not immune to the same illusion, since a class that has just reread its notes looks, and feels, better prepared than one that has just struggled to recall them. The method that feels like learning and the method that produces it are, at least here, not the same, and the lesson generalises uncomfortably: a learner's own sense of how well a session went is an unreliable guide to how much it achieved.

It would be easy to draw from all this a crude conclusion, that schools should simply test more, but the finding does not support it. What strengthens memory is the effort of retrieval, not the apparatus of examination, and the apparatus can work against the effort. A high-stakes test that provokes anxiety, or that is followed by no feedback, may teach students little except to fear tests, and a wrong answer recalled confidently and never corrected may itself be strengthened. The useful practice is humbler than the word 'test' suggests: it consists of frequent, low-stakes attempts to recall, each followed by a chance to check, built into ordinary study. None of this requires abolishing examinations, which serve purposes of certification that have little to do with memory; it requires only that they not be mistaken for the whole of what testing can do. Understood in this way, the thermometer turns out to be one of the more effective means of raising the temperature it was meant only to record.

options.A: Students who reread a passage felt more confident about a coming test than those who practised recall, although a week later they remembered less of it.
options.B: Students who sat a formal, high-stakes examination reported feeling far more anxious than students who practised recall at home with their books closed.
options.C: Answering recall questions improved memory a week later only when done under formal examination conditions, and not when done in an informal, ungraded session.
options.D: Students who received feedback after each attempt at recall remembered more a week later than students who attempted the same recall without any feedback.

passage: Architects tend to speak of a building as finished on the day it is handed over, and most architectural criticism shares the assumption. For its occupants, however, the handover is a beginning. Within a few years the first partitions have gone up or come down, a porch has been enclosed, a garage has become a bedroom, and the building has started to diverge from its drawings. A family grows and then shrinks, a business expands into the floor above, a school changes the way it teaches, and each of these shifts leaves its mark on the fabric. Over a century the divergence can be so complete that little of the original arrangement survives except the outer walls and the structural frame. If we want to know how well a building has been designed, the question of how it absorbs such changes deserves at least as much attention as the question of how it looked when new.

The obvious response is to design for change, and for several decades architects attempted exactly that. Offices and schools were built as open floors with movable partitions, and houses with walls that could slide, fold or be unbolted, so that occupants could rearrange the interior at will. The results were often disappointing. Movable partitions were seldom moved, because moving them was laborious and disturbed the services concealed within them; the flexible plan turned out to be a plan that suited no particular use well; and the occupants, rather than enjoying their freedom, filled the space with improvised screens and cabinets to make the rooms that the design had declined to provide. Designing for every possible use, it emerged, had been a way of designing for none.

The buildings that have in fact proved most adaptable are frequently ones that were never designed with change in mind. Old warehouses and mills, with their regular grids of columns, generous ceiling heights and thick, plain walls, have been turned into flats, studios, schools and offices with surprising ease. Terraced houses built for one family have been divided into apartments and, a generation later, joined up again. What these buildings share is not flexibility in the engineered sense but a kind of slack: dimensions a little larger than any one use required, a structure simple enough to be understood by ordinary builders, and surfaces that can be cut into without catastrophe. The ordinary builder called in to knock two rooms together can see at once where the loads run and what may safely be taken away. They fit their first use loosely, and that looseness is what lets them fit their later uses at all.

The lesson is an uncomfortable one for a profession that prides itself on precision. A building tailored exactly to its brief, every room sized to its programme and every service routed to suit it, is admirable on the day of opening and brittle thereafter, because the brief will change and the building cannot. Generosity of this kind costs something at the outset, in floor area and in height, and clients are seldom eager to pay for space that nobody has yet asked for. This is not an argument against all precision; an operating theatre or a laboratory must fit its use closely, and a little slack in the wrong place is merely waste. But for most ordinary buildings, which will outlive the purposes for which they were commissioned, the more durable virtue is a certain generosity, together with a willingness on the architect's part to regard the occupants' later alterations not as defacement but as the building continuing to do its job.

options.A: Most warehouses and mills were built without the slightest expectation that people would one day live or work in them.
options.B: Flexible-plan offices built in recent decades have been demolished far more often than old warehouses in the same districts.
options.C: Warehouses with low ceilings and irregular columns proved as easy to convert as those with generous ceilings and regular grids.
options.D: Some warehouses converted into flats were later returned to storage when the demand for housing in their district fell.

passage: A parent who hears a child begin a sentence in one language and finish it in another often worries that the child has learned neither properly. Teachers have voiced the same anxiety, and so, at times, have bilingual speakers themselves, who describe their own mixing with a kind of apology, as though it betrayed a laziness they ought to overcome. The assumption behind the worry is simple: a speaker who switches must be reaching for a word he does not have, and a speaker who is constantly reaching has not finished learning.

The assumption is not absurd, and sometimes it is true. Anyone who has lived between two languages knows the moment when the word for a kitchen utensil, or for a form at the bank, has been acquired in one language and simply not in the other. But careful recordings of bilingual conversation suggest that such gaps account for only part of what happens, and not the most interesting part. Switches tend to fall at points where the grammars of the two languages fit together and to avoid points where they clash, so that a sentence begun in one language and finished in another is usually well formed by the standards of both. A speaker who was merely groping for words would not be so tidy. To switch in this way, one needs to know two grammars well enough to sense, without thinking, where they can be joined.

Nor is the timing of a switch random. Speakers move into the other language to report what someone else said, to mark a change of topic, to soften a refusal, to signal that a remark is a joke, or to draw a listener in or shut one out. A grandmother's proverb may be quoted in the language she used, not because the speaker cannot translate it, but because the translation would lose the grandmother. In such uses the switch itself carries meaning, much as a change of tone does within a single language; it is a resource that monolingual speakers lack, not a failure that they have avoided.

None of this means that every setting must welcome mixing. An examination set in one language, or a document that must be read by people who know only one, may reasonably require a speaker to stay within it, and a bilingual who could not do so would indeed have a problem. The error lies in treating the ability to keep languages apart as the measure of competence, and the habit of combining them as its absence. Most bilinguals can do both. Judging them by the first alone is like judging a pianist only by whether she can play with one hand.

options.A: Judging a chess player only by her results in fast games, while ignoring her long and strong record in slow, classical games.
options.B: Grading a musician trained in two traditions only on how strictly she keeps them apart, and treating her blending of the two as poor training.
options.C: Requiring a surgeon to use only the instruments approved for a particular operation, although she is equally skilled with several others.
options.D: Praising a novelist for freely mixing genres even when readers report that the resulting books are hard to follow.

passage: Popular advice about habits tends to treat them as a contest of will. Bad habits persist, on this account, because people lack the resolve to stop, and good ones fail to form because people give up too soon. The remedy is accordingly motivational: set firmer goals, remind yourself why they matter, and try harder. This view has the appeal of moral simplicity, since it locates every failure in a lack of character and every success in effort, and it is repeated in a great deal of well-meant advice. The trouble with this picture is that it misdescribes what a habit is. A habit is not a desire that has grown strong but a response that has become attached to a context, so that the context itself, rather than any present intention, sets the behaviour going.

Consider someone who checks her phone each time she sits down on the morning train. At first the action may have been chosen, perhaps as a way of passing an otherwise idle part of the trip, but after hundreds of repetitions it no longer needs choosing. The seat, the motion of the carriage and the familiar stretch of the journey are enough to bring the hand to the pocket, and she may find the phone in her hand before she has formed any wish to look at it. Asking her to resolve more firmly misses the point, since resolve is not what produces the act. The cue is.

If this is right, the most effective way to change a habit is often to change the circumstances that trigger it, not to strengthen the will that opposes it. Putting the phone in a bag rather than a pocket, sitting in a different carriage, or giving the first minutes of the journey to some specific task all interrupt the link between cue and response. Each of these requires a single decision rather than a renewed act of resistance every morning, which is precisely why such changes tend to outlast good intentions. It is often observed that people find it easier to alter their routines after moving house or changing jobs, and the account explains why: the old cues have simply disappeared, and with them much of the pressure to repeat old behaviour.

Two cautions are in order, however, if the argument is not to be pushed further than it can go. First, not every repeated behaviour is a habit in this sense; some acts are repeated because the person goes on wanting the result each time, and for these, motivation does matter. Second, the power of context cuts both ways. The same disruption that frees someone from an unwanted routine can dissolve a welcome one, which is why a regular exercise habit so often lapses after a move. Willpower is not irrelevant, then, but it is a poor tool for a job that the environment, suitably arranged, performs more cheaply and more reliably.

options.A: the familiar features of the journey set off the action without any present decision by her.
options.B: she lacks the firmness of resolve that would allow her to keep the phone in her pocket.
options.C: she has a strong wish to look at it each time she sits down in the carriage.
options.D: she decided long ago that the journey was the right time for checking her messages.

passage: Discussions of antibiotic resistance usually begin with misuse: drugs prescribed for viral infections that they cannot touch, courses abandoned halfway, animals dosed to make them grow faster. Each of these practices gives bacteria more opportunities to evolve defences, and each deserves the attention it receives. Less often discussed is a quieter problem that has nothing to do with carelessness. Even if every prescription were perfectly judged, the way new antibiotics are paid for would discourage anyone from making them.

Consider what responsible use of a genuinely new antibiotic would look like. Because every use exerts selective pressure, the new drug should be held back for patients whose infections resist older and cheaper treatments, and it should be prescribed as rarely as possible for as long as possible. This is sound medicine. It is also a commercial disaster. A company recovers the cost of developing a drug by selling it in quantity during the years its patent protects it, and a drug that doctors are urged not to use cannot be sold in quantity. The contrast with a medicine for a chronic condition, taken every day for decades by millions of people, could hardly be sharper. It is not surprising that large firms have drifted out of the field, or that small firms that have brought new antibiotics through approval have sometimes failed commercially soon afterwards.

The proposed remedy is to separate a company's income from the number of doses it sells. Under such schemes, a health system would pay a fixed annual sum for access to a new antibiotic, whether it is used on a thousand patients or on ten, much as a town pays for a fire brigade whether or not anything burns that year. The payment rewards the existence of the drug rather than its consumption, which is exactly the property a reserve antibiotic is supposed to have.

The objections are real. Such payments are large, they must be justified to budget holders who see little use for their money, and nobody knows quite how to price a drug whose value lies mainly in emergencies it may never have to meet. Nor would better payment by itself guarantee discovery, since finding compounds that kill resistant bacteria without harming patients is scientifically hard. But these difficulties argue for designing the schemes carefully, not for abandoning them. The alternative is to go on rewarding a pattern of sales that good medicine forbids, and to discover the cost only when the older drugs have stopped working.

options.A: Medicines for chronic conditions cost more to develop than new antibiotics do, which gives their makers stronger incentives.
options.B: The price per course of a reserve antibiotic cannot be set high enough to recover its costs from a few patients.
options.C: Older and cheaper antibiotics will soon stop working against most common infections, leaving doctors with no alternative to the new drug.
options.D: A genuinely new antibiotic will usually prove less effective against common infections than the older and cheaper drugs it backs up.

passage: Collective security is one of those ideas that seem obviously right until one asks what they require. The principle is that an attack on any member of an international system is to be treated as an attack on all, so that every aggressor faces the combined strength of everyone else. Against this, the older practice of the balance of power looks cynical: states align against whichever power threatens to dominate, and they change sides as readily as the threat shifts, guided by interest rather than by any judgement about who is in the right.

The appeal of collective security lies in its impartiality, and so does its weakness. For the scheme to work, states must be willing to fight an aggressor regardless of who it is, which means fighting, if necessary, a friend, a major trading partner or a power whose goodwill they need elsewhere. They must also be willing to fight over places where they have no interest at all, because the principle admits no distinction between an attack that matters to them and one that does not. This is a great deal to ask of governments that answer to their own citizens, and the interwar experience suggests that, when the moment came, many would not pay the price. An organisation founded on the principle found its members ready to condemn aggression and reluctant to resist it.

The balance of power asks less and so delivers more reliably, at least within its narrower aims. It does not require states to care about aggression as such, only about the rise of a power that could threaten them, and so it draws on motives that governments actually have. But its reliability comes at a price. Because it attends only to the distribution of strength, it is indifferent to the fate of small states whose conquest does not upset the balance; it can tolerate, and has often arranged, the partition of a weak country as a way of keeping the strong ones satisfied. Stability is its aim, and justice enters only by accident.

The lesson is not that one principle should replace the other, but that each supplies what the other lacks. A norm against aggression, however imperfectly enforced, gives resistance to an expanding power a public justification and makes it easier to assemble allies who would hesitate to act on calculation alone. Balancing, in turn, supplies the motive that the norm cannot generate by itself. Orders that have lasted have usually combined the two, borrowing their legitimacy from the first and their enforcement from the second, and the mistake of the reformers who championed collective security was to imagine that legitimacy could do the work of both.

options.C: A group of states pledges to defend any member that is attacked and honours the pledge even against a small aggressor that could never threaten any of them.
options.D: A worldwide body votes by a large majority to condemn the invasion of a remote island and calls on its members to resist, but no member sends any forces.

passage: The mirror test has an appealing simplicity: an animal is given a mark it cannot see directly, perhaps a spot of odourless dye on the forehead, and is then shown a mirror. If it uses the reflection to inspect or rub at the mark on its own body, it is said to recognise itself. Great apes generally pass, most monkeys generally fail, and over the decades a handful of other species have been reported to pass or nearly pass. Because the result is so easy to state, it has come to be treated as a kind of membership test: those who pass belong among the self-aware, and those who fail are presumed to lack a self worth the name.

The test does measure something real. To pass, an animal must grasp that the moving figure in the glass is not another individual and that what it sees there corresponds to its own body. That is not a trivial achievement, and it is reasonable to think that animals capable of it have some representation of their own bodies as objects among others. The difficulty lies in what is inferred from failure, and in how much is read into success.

Consider failure first, since the test presupposes an animal that relies heavily on vision, that attends to its own appearance, and that is bothered enough by an odd mark to investigate it. Many animals meet none of these conditions. A dog, which navigates its world largely by smell, may simply have no interest in a silent image that gives off no scent; an animal whose species does not groom may see no reason to touch a spot on its skin. Failing a test designed around one animal's priorities is weak evidence that another animal lacks the capacity being tested, in the way that a person's failure to answer a question asked in an unfamiliar language reveals little about her knowledge.

Success is open to over-reading too. Recognising one's body in a mirror shows an understanding of the body as one's own; it does not show, by itself, that the animal reflects on its past, imagines its future or thinks of itself as a person with a history. These are richer capacities, and the leap from the mirror to them is a leap of interpretation, not of evidence. None of this makes the test worthless. It makes it one probe among many, informative within its range and silent outside it. The error is not in running the test but in letting a single, visually biased procedure decide which minds are admitted to the category of the self-aware.

options.A: Dogs that ignore their reflection sniff a sample of their own scent far longer when it has been altered with an added odour than when it is left unchanged.
options.B: Several species of monkey that fail the mirror test perform well on other tests of memory and problem solving.
options.C: Some animals that pass the mirror test go on to use mirrors to inspect parts of their bodies that they cannot otherwise see.
options.D: Animals that pass the mirror test also tend to live in large and complex social groups.

passage: Of all the performing arts, dance has the most fragile relation to its own past. A play survives in its script and a symphony in its score, so that later generations, whatever they make of these documents, at least have something to argue over. A dance, by contrast, has for most of its history existed only while it was being danced and in the memories of those who danced it. It is tempting to conclude that dance is therefore an art without a history, or one whose history is a long series of losses, and that the remedy is simply better documentation.

There have been serious attempts at such documentation. Systems of dance notation have been devised that record the position of each part of the body over time, and film and video now capture performances that would once have vanished. These tools are valuable, but they have not displaced the older method of transmission, in which a dancer who has performed a role teaches it directly to a younger dancer, in a studio, by demonstration and correction. Many companies that hold detailed records of their repertoire still rely on such teaching when a work is revived, and they tend to treat the written record as an aid to memory rather than as the work itself.

The reason is not mere conservatism. What passes from one body to another in the studio includes things that a notation or a recording captures poorly or not at all: the weight of a movement, the quality of attention behind it, the reasons a gesture is timed as it is. A film shows what a particular dancer did on a particular night, including her idiosyncrasies and her mistakes; it cannot say which of those features belong to the choreography and which belong to her. A teacher who has danced the role can make that distinction, or at least has a considered view about it, and passes the view on along with the steps.

This method has an obvious cost. Each transmission is also an interpretation, and over several generations a dance may drift a long way from what its maker first set. Yet the drift is not simply a corruption. A dance kept alive in bodies is continually tested against the dancers who perform it, and the features that survive are usually those that dancers have found to matter. The archive of dance, on this view, is not mainly a shelf of documents but a lineage of people, and its gaps are the price of its being alive.

options.B: convey the weight and timing of each movement more faithfully than a revival taught in the studio, since film records every detail.
options.C: fail chiefly because film cannot show the position of each part of the body over time.
options.D: risk copying one performer's personal habits and errors as though they were part of the choreography.

passage: The phrase 'conspicuous consumption', coined by Thorstein Veblen in the 1890s, named a habit of the wealthy of his day: the purchase of goods whose chief use was to show that one could afford them. The mansion, the carriage and the idle household were, on this account, less comforts than advertisements. The idea proved so useful that it outlived the society that prompted it, and it still shapes how we picture status spending: the logo on the handbag, the oversized car, the watch that costs more than a year's rent.

The picture now misleads more than it reveals, at least at the top. As mass production and global supply chains have made once-rare goods cheap, the handbag and the car have become available, in passable imitations, to almost anyone with a credit card. Display of this kind has lost much of its power to separate, and many of the most advantaged households have turned away from it. Their spending flows instead into things that are hard to see and harder to copy: private tuition and a house in the right school catchment, retirement savings, organic groceries, exercise classes, domestic help that frees time for reading, and clothing whose quality is recognised only by those who know what to look for. The signal, where there is one, is addressed to a narrow audience of peers rather than to the street. The pattern has come to be called inconspicuous consumption.

It would be easy to treat the change as an improvement in taste, a retreat from vulgar display into quieter and more sensible habits. In part it is. Much of this spending yields real benefits in health, in learning and in security, and few would wish the rich to return to buying gold-plated taps. But the shift has two consequences that the language of good taste conceals. The first is that inconspicuous goods are more effective at reproducing advantage than conspicuous ones ever were. A diamond can be sold; a childhood spent in good schools, with books at home and parents who have time, becomes part of a person and can neither be taken away nor easily acquired later. Spending of this kind does not merely display a position; it passes it on.

The second consequence is moral. Conspicuous consumption invited criticism precisely because it was conspicuous. The flashy car was an obvious target for the satirist and the moralist, and its owner could be accused of vanity. Inconspicuous consumption is much harder to criticise, because it presents itself not as display but as virtue: one is not showing off, one is merely eating well, looking after one's health and investing in one's children. The vocabulary that surrounds it, of wellness, sensible choices and doing the best for one's family, offers the satirist nothing obviously vulgar to mock. Those who cannot afford to do the same are not envied so much as quietly judged, as though their diets and their children's results were failures of character rather than of income.

None of this is an accusation of bad faith. It does not require us to think the affluent hypocritical, or the parent paying for tuition secretly bent on buying status; most such choices are made sincerely, for the reasons people give. The point is structural rather than personal. A society in which advantage is transmitted through the visible accumulation of objects at least makes its inequalities legible. One in which advantage flows through habits, schooling and time has made them harder to see, and inequalities that are hard to see are also harder to argue about.

passage: Ask people what grief involves and many will describe a sequence: denial, then anger, then bargaining, then depression, and at last acceptance. The sequence has become so familiar that it can seem like a discovery about human nature, as settled as the stages of a fever. It began, however, as a description of how some terminally ill patients responded to the news of their own approaching death, drawn from clinical conversations rather than from any systematic study of the bereaved. Its migration from the dying to the grieving, and from a set of observations to something closer to a timetable, happened largely outside the kind of research that might have tested it.

When grief has been studied directly, the tidy sequence has not fared well. Bereaved people commonly report several of the named feelings at once, or in no particular order, and many report some of them hardly at all. Perhaps the most striking finding is how many people cope with a loss far better than the model would lead one to expect, experiencing intense sorrow that gradually eases over months without passing through anything resembling distinct stages. Resilience of this kind is not denial in disguise; for a good number of people it seems simply to be the ordinary course that grief takes.

The harm of the model lies less in its inaccuracy than in what people do with it. A description of what some people feel becomes a standard of what everyone ought to feel, and departures from the standard begin to look like problems requiring attention. The widow who is not angry may be told that she has not yet faced her loss; the son who feels relief after a parent's long illness may wonder what is wrong with him. Friends, and even professionals, may wait for a stage that never arrives, or press a grieving person to move on to the next one as though grief were a course with a syllabus.

It would be unfair, though, to treat the model's popularity as mere credulity. It arrived at a time when dying and grief were seldom spoken of openly, and it gave people words for feelings, anger above all, that they might otherwise have hidden or been ashamed of. That was a real service, and it should not be forgotten in the rush to correct the record. The task now is to keep what the model offered, the permission to feel a wide range of things, while dropping the suggestion that those feelings must arrive in a fixed order, or arrive at all.

options.A: present evidence that the sequence accurately describes how terminally ill patients respond to their diagnosis.
options.B: argue that the stages of grief have never been observed in any patient or in any bereaved person.
options.C: explain why the experience of grief is much harder to study systematically than the experience of dying.
options.D: trace the familiar sequence back to an origin that differs from the use now made of it.

passage: Few ideas in economics are cited as often, or misunderstood as thoroughly, as comparative advantage. In everyday commentary trade is described as a contest: a country wins when it is better at making things than its rivals and loses when they overtake it. On this view a nation that is less productive than its neighbours in every industry would have nothing to sell and would be wise to close its borders. The principle of comparative advantage was formulated precisely to show why this conclusion does not follow, and the fact that the conclusion is still drawn suggests that the principle is more often invoked than understood.

The core insight concerns opportunity cost rather than absolute ability. Consider a hypothetical lawyer who types faster than any secretary she could hire. It does not follow that she should do her own typing, because every hour spent at the keyboard is an hour withdrawn from legal work that earns far more. The secretary, though slower at typing, gives up much less by doing it. Both are better off when each concentrates on the task in which his or her relative sacrifice is smallest and they exchange the results. The same reasoning applies to countries. What determines the pattern of trade is not which country is best at producing a good, but which country forgoes the least of other goods in producing it, and every country, however unproductive overall, has some activity in which that sacrifice is comparatively low.

Two consequences follow that sit uneasily with the language of contest. First, gains from trade do not require one party to lose: the lawyer and the secretary both gain, and so do a rich and a poor economy that trade on the basis of their differing costs. Second, a country cannot have a comparative advantage in everything, since being relatively better at one activity means, by definition, being relatively worse at another. A government that promises to make its nation competitive in every industry is therefore promising something that is not merely difficult but incoherent.

None of this implies that the critics of open trade have nothing to say. The textbook argument compares two settled states and is silent about the passage between them; workers who lose their jobs when an industry contracts do not costlessly reappear in the industry that expands, and the losses can be concentrated in particular towns for a generation. Comparative advantage can also shift over time as skills and capital accumulate, which is why some economists defend temporary support for new industries. These are serious objections, but they are objections to the timing and distribution of the gains, not to the logic of opportunity cost. They do not restore the image of trade as a race in which one runner's progress is another's defeat.

options.A: advise poorer countries to specialise in the industries where their workers are least productive in absolute terms.
options.B: demonstrate that open trade benefits every worker in every country, so that the objections raised by its critics can be safely set aside.
options.C: correct a popular misreading of comparative advantage, while granting objections that leave its logic of opportunity cost intact.
options.D: show that the critics of open trade have misunderstood the costs of moving workers from contracting industries into expanding ones.

passage: Arguments about gentrification tend to collapse into a single question: are the people who lived in a neighbourhood forced out when wealthier newcomers arrive? The question has the merit of being answerable, at least in principle. One can follow households over time, count how many leave, and compare the rate with that in neighbourhoods that have not changed. Suppose such a count found that long-standing residents of a gentrifying district left no faster than residents of similar districts elsewhere. Many would conclude that the harm of gentrification had been exaggerated, and that what remained of the complaint was mere nostalgia.

That conclusion would be premature, because it assumes that the only way to lose a neighbourhood is to leave it. Consider the resident who stays. The grocer who extended credit has been replaced by a shop whose prices assume another income; the bench outside it, once a place to sit for an afternoon, now draws the attention of a security guard; the park is the same park, but the conduct expected in it has quietly changed, and complaints to the police now come from people she does not know, about behaviour that was ordinary a decade ago. She has not moved, and no count of departures will register her, yet the place in which she lives has been withdrawn from her as surely as if she had. To call this nostalgia is to mistake a loss of standing for a loss of scenery.

The difficulty is that the language best suited to describing this loss, the language of a neighbourhood's 'character', is also the language most readily turned to the opposite purpose. Affluent districts invoke their character to resist new housing, to keep out flats that might bring poorer residents, to preserve a streetscape that functions, whatever its owners intend, as a barrier. If character means the look of the buildings and the tone of the streets, then the long-standing resident and the exclusionary homeowner are making the same argument, and it is not one that deserves much sympathy.

The way out is to locate character not in the fabric of a place but in the relations it sustains: who is able to use it, on what terms, and with what claim to be heard. On this view, what the staying resident has lost is not a familiar shopfront but the practical standing she once had in her own street, and what the exclusionary homeowner defends is not a set of relations at all but the absence of people who might form new ones. The distinction will not settle every case, and it asks more of planners than a count of departures does. But it allows us to take the quieter harms of gentrification seriously without lending our sympathy to every resident who would prefer that nothing near them ever changed.

options.A: Judging character by the relations a place sustains demands more of planners than counting those who leave.
options.B: A resident who stays in a gentrifying district loses more of her neighbourhood than one who is forced to leave it.
options.C: A count of departures, however careful, cannot register the losses of residents who remain in a changing district.
options.D: The same appeal to a neighbourhood's character can serve both to describe a genuine loss and to justify exclusion.

passage: When a welfare benefit goes unclaimed by many of the people entitled to it, the usual explanation is that they did not know about it, did not need it badly enough or could not be bothered. The explanation locates the problem in the claimant. It rarely asks what claiming actually involves: discovering that the benefit exists, working out whether one qualifies, gathering documents that may be held by three different offices, completing a form whose questions assume a settled address and a regular income, and then, often, doing it all again a few months later to prove that nothing has changed.

These demands are usually described as administrative friction, an unfortunate but neutral by-product of running any large programme. They are not neutral. Every hour required to claim is an hour that some people can spare more easily than others, and the people least able to spare it are frequently those the programme was meant to help: the seriously ill, those working irregular shifts, those for whom scarcity has already consumed much of the attention that form-filling demands. A requirement that costs a comfortable applicant an afternoon may cost a struggling one the benefit itself.

There is a further reason to look closely at such burdens. Because they are set through forms, procedures and office hours rather than through legislation, they can change who receives a benefit without any public decision that it should. A government that wished to spend less on a programme but did not wish to say so could add a document to the list or shorten the period for renewal, and the number of recipients would fall while the rules of entitlement stayed exactly as they were. Whether or not anyone intends this, the effect is a form of policy made out of sight, insulated from the debate that a change in the law would provoke.

This is not to say that verification is illegitimate. Public programmes depend on the belief that money goes to those entitled to it, and some checking sustains that belief among the taxpayers who fund them. But the costs of checking are borne in two places, in the office and in the lives of applicants, and only the first tends to be counted. A sound design would weigh the time and strain imposed on claimants as seriously as the cost of the errors it prevents, and would treat a large gap between entitlement and receipt as evidence about the system rather than about the people outside it.

options.A: The costs of verification fall partly on applicants, and these are often left out of the reckoning.
options.B: Burdens on claimants are introduced chiefly by governments that want to cut spending without public debate.
options.C: A fall in the number of people receiving a benefit need not reflect any change in the rules that define who is entitled to it.
options.D: A requirement that is a minor nuisance for one applicant may be decisive for another applicant.

passage: Virtue ethics asks not what rule an action follows or what outcome it produces but what kind of person performs it. Its central concepts are traits of character such as honesty, courage and compassion, conceived as stable dispositions that lead a person to act well across a wide range of circumstances. The compassionate person does not help only when it is convenient or when someone is watching; her compassion shows itself in the market and at home, towards friends and towards strangers. It is this breadth that distinguishes a virtue from a habit, and it is what makes the attribution of a virtue a substantial claim about a person rather than a summary of what she happened to do last week.

In recent decades a group of critics, often called situationists, has argued that this picture is empirically naive. They point to a body of experimental work in social psychology, some of it now disputed, which has been taken to show that small and morally irrelevant features of a situation, such as whether a person is in a hurry or in a pleasant mood, predict whether she will help someone in need far better than anything we know about her character. If behaviour is driven so heavily by circumstance, the critics conclude, then broad traits of the kind virtue ethics requires are rare or nonexistent, and a theory built around them describes a psychology that human beings do not have. On this view, to call someone honest or kind is less a discovery about her than a story we tell to make her conduct look more orderly than it is.

The argument is more damaging to some versions of virtue ethics than to others. If the theory claimed that most people possess the virtues, the evidence would tell heavily against it. But the classical tradition never claimed this. It held that full virtue is difficult, uncommon and achieved, if at all, through long training, and that most people are a mixture of good impulses and weak resolve. Evidence that ordinary people are easily swayed by circumstance is exactly what such a tradition would predict. Indeed, much of the advice it offers, to avoid temptations rather than trust oneself to resist them and to choose one's companions with care, makes sense only on the assumption that character is fragile.

This reply, however, has a cost that its defenders do not always acknowledge. If genuine virtue is so rare that experimental samples almost never contain it, then virtue ethics can no longer claim the advantage it has often advertised over its rivals: that it describes moral life as it is actually lived, in terms of real people and their recognisable qualities. An ideal that almost no one embodies may still be worth pursuing, but it begins to look less like a description of character and more like a rule of the kind the theory set out to replace, a standard against which conduct is measured rather than a source from which it flows.

The situationist challenge, then, does not refute virtue ethics, but it changes what the theory can coherently promise. The theory can keep its account of the ideal, or its claim to realism about ordinary people, but it is hard to see how it can keep both. Which it should give up is a question that experiments alone cannot answer, since it depends on what we want an ethical theory to do: to guide those who aspire to goodness, or to describe those whose characters are already formed.

options.A: A training programme grows more effective the more often its trainees repeat each of the exercises it prescribes.
options.B: A recipe that usually fails when beginners attempt it must have been written incorrectly by the cook who devised it.
options.C: A rulebook for a game can be replaced without loss by a description of how skilled players actually behave in matches.
options.D: A map can be drawn to show the route an expert ought to take or to record the paths walkers actually use, but hardly to do both at once.
